Table~\ref{tab:p1} lists pass counts and cost for the 12 configurations, and Figure~\ref{fig:p1pareto} plots
cost against solved runs. Over all four harnesses, GPT-6.1 Sol solved 65 of 160 runs (41\%, \$249.99, \$3.85 per
solve), Claude Sonnet~5.5 51 of 160 (32\%, \$135.76, \$2.66 per solve) and GLM-5.3 Flash 43 of 160 (27\%,
\$58.02, \$1.35 per solve).

\paragraph{The harness changes pass rate, cost and time (RQ1).}
With the model held fixed, the harness moved the number of solved runs from 4 to 16 of 40 for GLM-5.3 Flash,
from 10 to 16 for Sonnet~5.5 and from 14 to 18 for Sol. Changing the harness moved GLM's pass rate from 10\% (Codex
CLI) to 40\% (Claude Code), a difference of 30 percentage points. By comparison, when each model's runs are pooled
over all four harnesses, the strongest model (Sol, 41\%) and the weakest (GLM, 27\%) differ by 14 percentage
points. For Sol
the harness mostly moved cost: Sol solved 18 runs under Codex CLI for \$17.83 and 17 under ZCode for \$126.05,
seven times the cost for one solve fewer.

\paragraph{No single best harness (RQ1a).}
The ranking of harnesses depends on the model. Codex CLI was Sol's best harness (18 of 40), third for Sonnet
(11) and GLM's worst (4). ZCode was second for GLM and for Sol but last for Sonnet. Each provider's own harness
did well for its model: Codex for Sol, ZCode near the top for GLM and Claude Code at the top for Sonnet.
Claude Code was also at the top for GLM. Some of these rankings depend on very small differences. Sol's three best
harnesses, Codex CLI, ZCode and Claude Code, solved 18, 17 and 16 runs, only one run apart. Because repeated runs of
the same task often change between pass and fail, gaps of one or two runs are within run-to-run variance and
could reverse if the runs were repeated. Larger gaps, such as GLM's 16 solved runs under Claude Code against 4
under Codex CLI, are not explained by this variance.

\paragraph{A cheaper model in a matched harness (RQ1b).}
Choosing the harness can matter as much as choosing the model. In Claude Code all three models solved 16 of 40
runs, at \$0.63 per solve for GLM, \$1.39 for Sol and \$2.13 for Sonnet. In ZCode, GLM solved 15 runs against
Sonnet's 10. The trade-off is time: in Claude Code and ZCode, GLM's median run took 47 and 42 minutes, against 10
and 11 minutes for Sonnet in the same harnesses. In Figure~\ref{fig:p1pareto}, GLM in Claude Code and Sol in Codex
CLI form the cost--solve frontier: no other configuration solves more runs at a lower cost.

\paragraph{Reliability.}
The harness also decides whether a run finishes at all. GLM gave no result in 7 of 40 runs under Hermes, against
0 to 3 under the other harnesses. Over all harnesses, 13 GLM runs and 11 Sol runs (6 of them under Claude Code)
ended without a result; every Sonnet run produced one. These runs count as not passed.

\paragraph{Run-to-run variance.}
Agents are not deterministic: the same model, harness and task can pass once and fail the next time. Each
configuration ran three tasks three times (Appendix~\ref{app:p1}). In 12 of these 36 groups the outcome
flipped between pass and fail, and 2 more changed only because a run gave no result. We therefore treat gaps of
one or two tasks as possible noise and call a difference real only when it is larger.
